name: Inspect a kubeadm cluster
objective: CKA › Cluster Architecture, Installation & Configuration (25%). Drill EVERY node-level kubeadm corner harder than the exam: inspect component versions, read the kubelet config and static-pod manifests, mint a worker join token, perform the drain/uncordon maintenance dance, renew control-plane certificates, read an upgrade plan, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. All graded exactly on persistent node/cluster state.

questions.title: Inspect component versions
questions.teach:
Before any upgrade, read what you're running. `kubeadm version -o short` prints the CLI tag; `kubelet --version` prints `Kubernetes v...`. Both binaries live on the node, so reach them with `docker exec` into $CP.

**Gotcha:** a redirect like `docker exec "$CP" kubelet --version > /tmp/f` writes to YOUR host, not the node — redirect INSIDE the node: `docker exec "$CP" sh -c '... > /tmp/f'`.
questions.prompt:
On the control-plane node ($CP), capture the kubeadm and kubelet versions and write BOTH, one per line, to `/tmp/versions.txt` on $CP.

Target: `docker exec "$CP" cat /tmp/versions.txt` shows a `kubeadm`/`v…` line and a `Kubernetes v...` (kubelet) line.
questions.hint: Redirect INSIDE the node: `docker exec "$CP" sh -c 'kubeadm version -o short > /tmp/versions.txt; kubelet --version >> /tmp/versions.txt'`. Confirm with `docker exec "$CP" cat /tmp/versions.txt`.
questions.solution:
docker exec "$CP" sh -c 'kubeadm version -o short > /tmp/versions.txt; kubelet --version >> /tmp/versions.txt'
docker exec "$CP" cat /tmp/versions.txt

verification.description: /tmp/versions.txt on $CP has a kubeadm version line + a kubelet 'Kubernetes v...' line

questions.eli5:
Imagine your cluster is a car you're about to take in for a service. Before you order any parts, the first thing you do is pop the hood and read the sticker that says exactly which engine and which model year you've got. If you guess wrong, you'll order the wrong parts and make things worse.

A **kubeadm** cluster is the same. Two separate pieces of software live on each node, and each has its own version:

- **kubeadm** — the tool that *builds and upgrades* the cluster. `kubeadm version -o short` prints its tag, like `v1.31.0`.
- **kubelet** — the agent that actually *runs pods* on the node. `kubelet --version` prints `Kubernetes v1.31.0`.

You want both written down before you touch anything.

Here the binaries live *inside* the node (a container called `$CP`), so you reach in with `docker exec "$CP" <command>` — like using a long robot arm to press buttons inside a sealed box.

**Watch out for:**

- **Redirects go to the wrong machine.** `docker exec "$CP" kubelet --version > /tmp/f` saves the file on **your** laptop, not inside the node — the `>` is handled by your shell. Put the redirect *inside* the box: `docker exec "$CP" sh -c 'kubelet --version > /tmp/f'`.
- **kubeadm and kubelet versions can differ.** Don't assume one tells you the other — read both.
- Use `>>` (append) for the second line, or you'll overwrite the first.
- `kubeadm version` without `-o short` prints a long struct; `-o short` gives just the tag.
questions.deepDive:
## Inspecting kubeadm component versions — full rundown

### Mental model
A kubeadm cluster is a set of versioned pieces. Before any upgrade you must know **what you're running**, because the upgrade sequence and skew rules depend on it. Two binaries live on every node, each with its own version:

- **kubeadm** — the lifecycle tool (`init`, `join`, `upgrade`, `certs`, `token`).
- **kubelet** — the node agent that runs pods and talks to the API server.

The control-plane *also* runs `kube-apiserver`, `kube-controller-manager`, `kube-scheduler` and `etcd` as static Pods, each with its own image tag. The "cluster version" people usually mean is the **kube-apiserver** version (what `kubectl version` reports as *Server Version*).

### The commands
```bash
# kubeadm CLI version — short form prints just the tag
kubeadm version -o short          # v1.31.0
kubeadm version                   # full struct (GitVersion, GoVersion, ...)
kubeadm version -o yaml|json      # machine-readable

# kubelet version — note the "Kubernetes " prefix
kubelet --version                 # Kubernetes v1.31.0

# server (apiserver) version from the API
kubectl version                   # shows Client + Server Version
kubectl version -o json | jq -r .serverVersion.gitVersion
```

Reaching binaries that live inside a node (kind runs nodes as containers):
```bash
docker exec "$CP" kubeadm version -o short
docker exec "$CP" kubelet --version

# write BOTH lines to a file INSIDE the node
docker exec "$CP" sh -c 'kubeadm version -o short >  /tmp/versions.txt; \
                         kubelet --version       >> /tmp/versions.txt'
docker exec "$CP" cat /tmp/versions.txt
```

### Version output cheat-sheet
| Command | Typical output | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `kubeadm version -o short` | `v1.31.0` | bare tag, ideal for scripting |
| `kubeadm version` | `kubeadm version: &version.Info{...}` | verbose Go struct |
| `kubelet --version` | `Kubernetes v1.31.0` | always prefixed with `Kubernetes ` |
| `kubectl version -o json` | `.serverVersion.gitVersion` | the running apiserver version |

### Version skew rules (why versions matter)
| Component | Allowed skew vs kube-apiserver |
|---|---|
| kube-apiserver (other instances in HA) | within 1 minor |
| kube-controller-manager / scheduler | no newer than apiserver, up to 1 minor older |
| kubelet | up to **3 minor** versions older (1.28+); never newer than apiserver |
| kubectl | within 1 minor of apiserver (±1) |
| kubeadm | matches the version you're upgrading to; can be 1 minor newer than current cluster |

**Upgrade order to remember:** you upgrade **one minor version at a time** — you cannot jump 1.29 → 1.31 directly. Upgrade `kubeadm` first, then `kubeadm upgrade apply`, then the `kubelet`/`kubectl` packages.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Shell redirects run on the host, not the node.** `docker exec "$CP" cmd > /tmp/f` writes to your machine. Wrap it: `docker exec "$CP" sh -c 'cmd > /tmp/f'`.
- Use `>>` for the second line or you overwrite the first.
- `kubeadm version` without `-o short` dumps a struct — graders/scripts usually want the short tag.
- kubelet output includes the word `Kubernetes`; don't strip it if the target asks for a `Kubernetes v...` line.
- The **kubeadm** binary version is **not** automatically the cluster version — the apiserver image tag is the source of truth for "what the cluster runs".

### Quick reference
```bash
docker exec "$CP" sh -c 'kubeadm version -o short > /tmp/versions.txt; \
                         kubelet --version >> /tmp/versions.txt'
docker exec "$CP" cat /tmp/versions.txt
# kubeadm: v1.31.0
# Kubernetes v1.31.0
```

questions.title: Read the kubelet's config file
questions.teach:
A kubeadm node's kubelet is driven by `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` (a `KubeletConfiguration`). The `cgroupDriver` there MUST match the container runtime's — a mismatch stops the kubelet from starting. Read the file on the node with `docker exec`.

**Gotcha:** this is the component config, NOT the `kubeadm-config` ConfigMap in kube-system — don't confuse the two.
questions.prompt:
On $CP, read `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` and write ONLY the value of its `cgroupDriver` field (e.g. `systemd` or `cgroupfs`) to `/tmp/cgroupdriver.txt` on $CP.

Target: `/tmp/cgroupdriver.txt` on $CP contains exactly the cgroupDriver value, nothing else.
questions.hint: Grep the field inside the node and strip the key: `docker exec "$CP" sh -c "grep cgroupDriver /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | awk '{print \$2}' > /tmp/cgroupdriver.txt"`. Confirm with `docker exec "$CP" cat /tmp/cgroupdriver.txt`.
questions.solution:
docker exec "$CP" sh -c "grep cgroupDriver /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | awk '{print \$2}' > /tmp/cgroupdriver.txt"
docker exec "$CP" cat /tmp/cgroupdriver.txt
questions.eli5:
Think of the **kubelet** as the building manager who runs the whole apartment block (the node). When the building is first set up by kubeadm, the manager is handed a thick rulebook — `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` — that tells them exactly how to do their job: how to carve up the heating and electricity, where to send logs, and so on.

One line in that rulebook is the **`cgroupDriver`**. "cgroups" are how Linux divides up CPU and memory between programs. There are two ways to manage them: `systemd` and `cgroupfs`. The catch is that the **container runtime** (the thing that actually launches containers, like containerd) has its own opinion about which method to use — and the manager and the runtime *must agree*. If one says "systemd" and the other says "cgroupfs," the kubelet refuses to start the building at all.

So your job here is simple: open the rulebook, find that one line, and write down just its value (`systemd` or `cgroupfs`).

**Watch out for:**

- **Two different "configs" sound alike — don't mix them up.** This file, `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`, is the kubelet's *component config*. There's a *separate* `kubeadm-config` ConfigMap stored inside the cluster (in the `kube-system` namespace) — that's kubeadm's cluster settings, not this.
- A **cgroupDriver mismatch** between kubelet and the runtime is a classic reason a node goes `NotReady` — the kubelet keeps crashing.
- The file lives *inside* the node, so read it with `docker exec "$CP" cat ...`, not from your laptop.
- Write *only* the value (`systemd`), not the whole `cgroupDriver: systemd` line, if that's what's asked.
questions.deepDive:
## The kubelet config file — full rundown

### Mental model
On a kubeadm node the kubelet is driven mostly by a **`KubeletConfiguration`** object serialized to a file at **`/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`**. kubeadm writes this file during `init`/`join`. A handful of host-specific flags live separately (see below), but the bulk of behaviour — cgroup driver, DNS, eviction thresholds, TLS, the static-pod path — is in this single YAML.

### Where kubelet configuration comes from
| Source | Path / location | Contains |
|---|---|---|
| **Component config** | `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` | the `KubeletConfiguration` (cgroupDriver, clusterDNS, evictionHard, staticPodPath, authentication…) |
| **Per-node flags** | `/var/lib/kubelet/kubeadm-flags.env` | node-specific `KUBELET_KUBEADM_ARGS` (e.g. `--container-runtime-endpoint`, `--node-ip`) |
| **systemd drop-in** | `/etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf` | tells systemd to load the two files above |
| **cluster-wide copy** | ConfigMap `kubelet-config` in `kube-system` | kubeadm's stored template, re-applied on upgrade |

> Do **not** confuse these with the **`kubeadm-config`** ConfigMap in `kube-system`, which holds `ClusterConfiguration`/`InitConfiguration` — kubeadm's cluster settings, not kubelet runtime config.

### The cgroupDriver field
```yaml
# /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml  (excerpt)
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
cgroupDriver: systemd          # MUST match the container runtime's driver
clusterDNS:
- 10.96.0.10
clusterDomain: cluster.local
staticPodPath: /etc/kubernetes/manifests
```

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `systemd` | kubelet delegates cgroup management to systemd (recommended default) |
| `cgroupfs` | kubelet writes the cgroup filesystem directly |

The kubelet's `cgroupDriver` **must equal** the container runtime's cgroup driver (containerd: `SystemdCgroup = true` in `/etc/containerd/config.toml`). A mismatch leaves the node unstable — kubelet fails to start or pods won't run, and the node shows `NotReady`.

### Reading it on a kind node
```bash
docker exec "$CP" cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml

# pull just the cgroupDriver value, write it INSIDE the node
docker exec "$CP" sh -c \
  "grep cgroupDriver /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | awk '{print \$2}' > /tmp/cgroupdriver.txt"
docker exec "$CP" cat /tmp/cgroupdriver.txt     # -> systemd
```

### Changing kubelet config (for context)
After editing `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` you must restart the kubelet:
```bash
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl restart kubelet
journalctl -u kubelet -f        # watch it come back
```
On upgrade, `kubeadm upgrade` refreshes the `kubelet-config` ConfigMap and `kubeadm upgrade node` re-writes the local file.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Component config vs cluster config:** `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` (this file) ≠ `kubeadm-config` ConfigMap. A classic trap.
- **cgroupDriver mismatch** is a top cause of `NotReady` nodes — kubelet and runtime must agree.
- Editing the file does nothing until `systemctl restart kubelet`.
- The file is on the **node**, not in the API — read it with `docker exec`/SSH, not `kubectl`.
- If asked for the *value only*, strip the key: output `systemd`, not `cgroupDriver: systemd`.
- Debugging a dead kubelet: `systemctl status kubelet` and `journalctl -xeu kubelet`.

### Quick reference
```bash
docker exec "$CP" grep cgroupDriver /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
# cgroupDriver: systemd
# runtime must match:  containerd -> SystemdCgroup = true
# restart after edits: systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet
```

questions.title: Read a static Pod manifest
questions.teach:
The control-plane components run as **static Pods** — the kubelet starts them straight from manifest files in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` (no API server needed). `kube-apiserver.yaml` there pins the apiserver's exact image, which is the version an upgrade bumps.

**Gotcha:** editing these files restarts the component immediately — here you only READ, so don't modify them.
questions.prompt:
On $CP, read `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` and write the apiserver container's full `image:` value (e.g. `registry.k8s.io/kube-apiserver:v1.31.0`) to `/tmp/apiserver-image.txt` on $CP.

Target: `/tmp/apiserver-image.txt` on $CP contains an image reference ending in a `kube-apiserver:v<major>.<minor>.<patch>` tag.
questions.hint: Pull the image line inside the node: `docker exec "$CP" sh -c "grep 'image:' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | awk '{print \$2}' > /tmp/apiserver-image.txt"`. Confirm with `docker exec "$CP" cat /tmp/apiserver-image.txt`.
questions.solution:
docker exec "$CP" sh -c "grep 'image:' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | awk '{print \$2}' > /tmp/apiserver-image.txt"
docker exec "$CP" cat /tmp/apiserver-image.txt

verification.description: /tmp/apiserver-image.txt on $CP holds the kube-apiserver image:tag from the static manifest

questions.eli5:
Here's a chicken-and-egg puzzle: the **API server** is the brain of Kubernetes — nothing gets scheduled without it. But if the API server itself is a pod, who starts *it* before the brain is even awake?

The answer is **static Pods**. Think of the kubelet (the node's building manager) as having a special "autostart folder" on disk: **`/etc/kubernetes/manifests/`**. The manager watches that folder like a hawk. Any YAML file you drop in there, it immediately starts as a pod — no API server, no scheduler, nobody else needed. It's like the Startup folder on an old Windows PC: put a shortcut there and it launches automatically on boot.

That's exactly how the control plane bootstraps itself. The files `kube-apiserver.yaml`, `kube-controller-manager.yaml`, `kube-scheduler.yaml`, and `etcd.yaml` sit in that folder, and the kubelet brings them up on its own.

Inside `kube-apiserver.yaml` there's an `image:` line — that pins the *exact version* of the API server, like `registry.k8s.io/kube-apiserver:v1.31.0`. When you upgrade the cluster, this is the line that changes.

**Watch out for:**

- **Editing these files is live and instant.** Save a change and the kubelet restarts that component *right now*. Here you only READ — don't modify.
- A typo in a static-pod manifest can take down your API server. Handle with care.
- These pods show up in `kubectl get pods -n kube-system` with the **node name appended** (e.g. `kube-apiserver-cp`) — that suffix is the tell that it's a static pod.
- You can't `kubectl delete` a static pod away — the kubelet just recreates it. Remove the file from the folder instead.
questions.deepDive:
## Static Pods & control-plane manifests — full rundown

### Mental model
A **static Pod** is a Pod the **kubelet** runs directly from a manifest file on disk — **no API server, no scheduler, no controller** involved. The kubelet watches a directory and reconciles the Pods there. This is how a kubeadm cluster solves the bootstrap chicken-and-egg problem: the control-plane components (apiserver, controller-manager, scheduler, etcd) are static Pods, so they can start **before** the API server exists.

### Where they live
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Manifest directory | `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` |
| Configured by | `staticPodPath` in `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` |
| Watched by | the kubelet (polls the directory) |
| Control-plane files | `kube-apiserver.yaml`, `kube-controller-manager.yaml`, `kube-scheduler.yaml`, `etcd.yaml` |

### The "mirror Pod"
For each static Pod, the kubelet creates a read-only **mirror Pod** in the API server so you can *see* it with `kubectl` — but you can't control it there:
```bash
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
# kube-apiserver-<nodename>      1/1  Running
# etcd-<nodename>                1/1  Running
```
The **`-<nodename>` suffix** is the signature of a static/mirror Pod. Deleting the mirror Pod with `kubectl delete` does nothing lasting — the kubelet immediately recreates it from the file.

### Reading the apiserver image
```bash
docker exec "$CP" cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# pull the image:tag, write it INSIDE the node
docker exec "$CP" sh -c \
  "grep 'image:' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | awk '{print \$2}' > /tmp/apiserver-image.txt"
docker exec "$CP" cat /tmp/apiserver-image.txt
# registry.k8s.io/kube-apiserver:v1.31.0
```
The `image:` tag is the component's exact version — this is precisely what `kubeadm upgrade apply` rewrites to bump the control plane.

### Lifecycle (add / change / remove)
| Action | Effect |
|---|---|
| Drop a file into `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` | kubelet starts the Pod within seconds |
| Edit a file in place | kubelet **restarts** that Pod immediately with the new spec |
| Remove the file | kubelet **stops** and removes the Pod |
| `kubectl delete pod` the mirror | recreated instantly — file is source of truth |

```yaml
# /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml (excerpt)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: kube-apiserver
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  containers:
  - name: kube-apiserver
    image: registry.k8s.io/kube-apiserver:v1.31.0
    command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --advertise-address=172.18.0.2
    - --etcd-servers=https://127.0.0.1:2379
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Edits are live and instant.** Saving a broken manifest can take down the API server — back it up first (`cp kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/`). In an inspect task, only read.
- You **cannot manage static Pods via `kubectl`** — edit the file on the node. `kubectl delete` only removes the mirror, which reappears.
- The `staticPodPath` is `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` on kubeadm clusters; a custom kubelet could set a different path — check `config.yaml` if unsure.
- A static Pod is tied to **one node** (the kubelet that reads the file); it never reschedules elsewhere.
- Common break-glass fix: a crashlooping apiserver is often a bad flag in `kube-apiserver.yaml` — move the file out, let it settle, fix, move it back.

### Quick reference
```bash
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/                       # etcd, apiserver, cm, scheduler
docker exec "$CP" grep image: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep "$CP"         # mirror pods, -<node> suffix
# staticPodPath set in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
```
